Scaling up the system using a 0.5 L bioreactor, we controlled O at around 20% without 2 pH control, as ethylene glycol production does not significantly affect pH. Initial formaldehyde concentration was set at 5 mM, with 5 mM formaldehyde fed every 0.5 hours and 20 mM formate every 3 hours (Figure 35 C-F). The ethylene glycol titer increased rapidly until 6 hours, similar to the deep-well plates. It then slowed down and plateaued at 8 hours, achieving a final titer of around 18 mM. Glycolaldehyde levels remained stable, while glycolate levels suddenly increased at 7 hours. The sudden increase in glycolate levels at 7 hours can be attributed to several factors. The conversion of glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol by glycolaldehyde reductase requires NADH. If NADH levels drop due to increased demand or insufficient regeneration, the pathway might shift towards the endogenous oxidase pathway, converting glycolaldehyde to glycolate. Formate dehydrogenase plays a crucial role in regenerating NADH from formate. If the enzyme's activity decreases, NADH regeneration may become insufficient, forcing more glycolaldehyde to be converted to glycolate. Over time, metabolic shifts within the cells might affect the expression or activity of formate dehydrogenase, altering NADH production rates, which can cause glycolaldehyde to be diverted toward glycolate production. Increased production rates or other metabolic activities might heighten the demand for NADH, outpacing its regeneration via formate dehydrogenase and leading to a shift towards glycolate formation. We chose to shorten the sampling time to obtain more accurate formaldehyde kinetics. Results showed that formaldehyde consumption was linear between 20 and 100 minutes, with a calculated consumption rate of 0.062 mM per minute. This indicates that 1.86 mM of formaldehyde would be consumed every half hour (Figure 36A).
